items.title: Introducing Geist Serif
items.summary: Geist started as a monospace typeface for developers, built for the editors and terminals where they spend their day doing their work. From there it grew into Geist Sans for product interfaces, and then into Geist Pixel, which was inspired by the grids of early computer screens.Today, we're adding a new member to the family: .Geist SerifGeist Serif is a high-contrast display serif built on the same foundations as Geist Sans, Geist Mono, and Geist Pixel. It has fine, saw-toothed serifs and sharp hairlines, and it was drawn to communicate messages powerfully both in the physical world and on the high-density screens on modern devices.At Vercel, Geist Sans runs the product. For headlines, though, we wanted a second voice, one that belongs to the same system, instead of a stranger picked from a drop-down menu.A lot of tech brands have moved away from clean sans-serifs to get some personality back, and many of them borrow from vintage computer ads. Geist Serif takes a different path: toward fashion, editorial design, and magazine headlines. It's our homage to the artists behind  and .Rolling StoneHarper's BazaarFrom the beginning, each Geist family has read from a chapter of type history: the Swiss design movement, early terminal and DOS computing, and now editorial print.Geist Serif began as a set of sketches by , which Andrés Briganti then expanded. The first letters already showed an expressive serif, in the spirit of typefaces like Victor Serif and Stanley.Evil RabbitWhen Mark Davis took over the drawings, we made the first release a display face for headlines, posters, and other large sizes, while work on the full family continued. Print has always struggled to hold fine hairlines and sharp serifs, but today's displays can handle a high level of detail. We wanted the new face to take full advantage of modern screens, so we thinned every downstroke by 50% and tightened the sidebearings to push the contrast as far as it would go.Each serif has a wedge on one side and a curve on the other, so the proportions are classical and look beautiful in print, but the construction is new and optimized for digital devices.The first prototype of Geist Serif was shared on April 1, 2026. Here's the same word, Geist, in that prototype, compared with the display drawing shipping today.The goal was to honor our original intent and keep the serif closely tied to the sans, even when the letters sit on top of each other. Geist Serif’s stems match Geist Sans, and the two share widths and postures.The saw-toothed serifs and high contrast give Geist an editorial voice. One phrase kept coming up as each character was drawn: “Geist grew teeth.”Geist Serif uses the same cap height and x-height as Geist Sans, so you can drop it into any Geist layout without moving a line. Mix Sans, Mono, Pixel, and Serif in the same sentence and every word looks the same size.Like Geist Pixel, Geist Serif has a variable axis that swaps the shape of every dot in the font, including those on  and  and in punctuation. The axis is called Element Shape (), and it gives you four variants: Regular with round dots (the default), Square, Triangle (a nod to the Vercel logo), and Heart.ijELSHEach variant also ships as its own static file. If you use the variable font, pick a variant with :font-variation-settingsIn July the font had . It now has  and covers 352 Latin-script languages, and we worked through more than 52,000 kerning pairs to get the spacing right. Some of the details are tiny. The eye of the , for example, is tilted exactly 7°.227 glyphs894gGeist Serif ships with:Geist Serif ships in the same package as the rest of the family:Exports and CSS variables:Each one has its own entry point, so you only ship the font file you use. For example, in  with :layout.tsxGeistSerifRegularYou can also download the font files, test every stylistic set, and inspect each glyph at .vercel.com/fontRegular is the first style we’re releasing, and the rest of the family is already in progress. We’re testing future versions while building this one, so this release is just the start.The variable font will range from Thin (100) to Black (900). In this week’s proofs, the g in Black is the letter we can’t stop looking at.To explore a text version, we built a foundry tool that measures strokes, including where they meet, and thickens the display outlines. It edits the outlines directly, so we can set real words and see which strokes need more weight.We’re also developing an italic generated entirely in Python. We slanted existing italics back upright and compared them with their romans. With the angle removed, the remaining differences show up clearly, and we turned them into rules we can test and revise. This italic won’t be the final version, but breaking glyphs in code helps us find the limits faster.Cyrillic support is planned to match Geist Sans and Geist Mono, and Geist Serif will come to Google Fonts after launch.With Geist Sans, Geist Mono, Geist Pixel, and now Geist Seri

items.title: Add liveness checks to your Daemons
items.summary: now support configuring HTTP liveness checks.Vercel DaemonsStart with an HTTP endpoint in your daemon that reports its health. Keep it lightweight so it responds quickly, and have it return an error status when the daemon is no longer healthy:The daemon configuration now accepts a  value pointing at that endpoint:livenessProbeVercel periodically requests the endpoint and restarts the daemon's container when the check fails, catching a daemon that is still running but no longer healthy. for more information about liveness checks, including default values and the optional tuning fields.Read the Daemon documentationRead more
